topic: roast vegetables steaming instead of browning
caption:
If your roast vegetables come out pale and a bit sad, nothing is wrong with your oven. They're steaming in their own water — and four small things fix it.

Save this before Sunday.
caption_fb: If your roast vegetables come out pale and soft, they're steaming in their own water rather than roasting. Four fixes.
first_comment: Crowding the tray is the one everybody does. Two trays, always.

slides.headline: Your vegetables are steaming, not roasting.
slides.subhead: Pale, soft, a little watery. The oven is fine — the *tray* is the problem.
slides.alt: Cover: your vegetables are steaming, not roasting

slides.headline: The tray is crowded
slides.body: Vegetables release water as they heat. Packed together, that water has nowhere to go, so they sit and *poach* in it. Use two trays.
slides.alt: A crowded tray traps moisture and poaches the vegetables

slides.headline: Browning needs real heat
slides.body: Below about 200°C the surface never dries fast enough to colour. Hot oven, single layer, no lid, no foil.
slides.alt: Roast at 220 degrees celsius for proper browning

slides.headline: You put them in wet
slides.body: Water on the surface has to boil off before anything can brown. Dry them properly after washing — *then* oil them.
slides.alt: Wet vegetables must dry before they can brown

slides.headline: Four fixes, in order
items: Dry them before the oil goes on
One layer, two trays if needed

slides.quote: Every time you turn them early, you trade a crust for a stir.
slides.alt: Pull quote about turning vegetables too early

slides.headline: Cook it better on Sunday
slides.body: Technique breakdowns three times a week, food and fashion both.
